message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel numeric work – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific, machine‑learning, and crypto tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each core is powerful, with deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, large caches, and complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of lightweight cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups; each core is simpler but many can run the same instruction simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, rich ISA (x86, ARM, etc.) with support for branching, exceptions, virtual memory, etc. | Often a reduced ISA focused on arithmetic and data movement; some GPUs have their own shader languages (HLSL/GLSL). |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, fast access to main RAM via a single memory controller. | Small per‑core caches; relies heavily on high‑bandwidth shared memory (VRAM) and specialized cache hierarchies (texture units, constant buffers). |
| **Parallelism** | Fine‑grained, task‑level parallelism (multi‑threading, multi‑process). | Coarse‑grained, data‑parallelism (SIMD across thousands of threads). |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential code, decision trees, I/O bound tasks, operating system services. | Matrix/vector math, image/video processing, neural network inference/training, simulations that can be expressed as many independent operations over arrays. |
| **Power & cost** | More power‑efficient per core for general tasks; cheaper to build one or two CPUs than hundreds of GPU cores. | High throughput per watt when running massively parallel kernels; cost scales with number of cores and VRAM. |

In short, a CPU excels at handling diverse, irregular tasks with low latency, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation millions of times in parallel—exactly what’s required for modern graphics and AI workloads.
